name: Honolulu
garrison_1941: Fort Shafter (the Hawaiian Department's headquarters), the Diamond Head batteries of Fort Ruger, Fort DeRussy (hedged)
garrison_peak: with Pearl Harbor, two Army divisions and more (historian, for Oahu)
history: Struck from the air 7 Dec 1941 (Kaneohe and Bellows with Pearl Harbor); never landed on
check: Clerk 17 Nov: Oahu's second province. Works 1 is the clerk's split of the historian's 2 for Oahu (the Diamond Head batteries); fields split by where they lie (John Rodgers, Kaneohe naval air station, Bellows: an airfield) Floor checked by the historian 17 Nov: half stands.
notes: Capital of the Territory of Hawaii (a territory's seat, not a government's, so not a capital). About 180,000 people in 1940. Honolulu Harbor is the commercial port; the fleet base is Pearl Harbor next door.

name: Maui
history: Kahului shelled by a submarine 31 Dec 1941; never landed on; the 4th Marine Division trained and rested here 1944 to 1945
check: Chief place: Wailuku was the county seat and, with Kahului's harbour, the chief town; the map builder suggested Lahaina, the old royal town Floor (ruling 181) is the clerk's: the planner's file has no value for it. Floor checked by the historian 17 Nov: half, as the clerk proposed.
notes: Field in 1941: the Puunene airport (1938); the Navy's Puunene and Kahului air stations came 1942 to 1943. Haleakala rises to 3,000 m; the isthmus between is cane land. Its harbour is a commercial one, not a fleet base. Historian 17 Nov: floor half: cane and pineapple land could be turned to food, and the islands had ranches; Hawaii imported most of its food in 1941 only by choice of crop.

name: Hawaii
garrison_peak: the 2nd and 5th Marine Divisions' camp (Camp Tarawa, near Waimea), 1944 (hedged)
history: Hilo shelled by a submarine 30 Dec 1941; never landed on
check: Floor (ruling 181) is the clerk's: the planner's file has no value for it. Floor checked by the historian 17 Nov: half, as the clerk proposed.
notes: Rain all year on the windward side round Hilo; the Kona side is dry. Hilo's field was an Army landing ground in 1941. Mauna Loa and Mauna Kea above 4,000 m. Its harbour is a commercial one, not a fleet base. Historian 17 Nov: floor half: cane and pineapple land could be turned to food, and the islands had ranches; Hawaii imported most of its food in 1941 only by choice of crop.

name: Kauai
garrison_peak: an Army division in training, 1942 to 1944 (hedged)
history: Nawiliwili shelled by a submarine 31 Dec 1941; a Japanese pilot from the Pearl Harbor raid came down on Niihau 7 Dec 1941; never landed on
check: Floor (ruling 181) is the clerk's: the planner's file has no value for it. Floor checked by the historian 17 Nov: half, as the clerk proposed.
notes: Harbours at Nawiliwili and Port Allen; fields at Burns Field and Mana (Barking Sands) in 1941. Mount Waialeale is among the wettest places on earth. Its harbour is a commercial one, not a fleet base. Historian 17 Nov: floor half: cane and pineapple land could be turned to food, and the islands had ranches; Hawaii imported most of its food in 1941 only by choice of crop.

name: Anchorage
check: Seward (the railway's ice-free port) and the Kenai Peninsula are taken to lie in this province: the harbour is Seward's, as Anchorage's own wharf on Cook Inlet iced up in winter Spot-checked by the historian 17 Nov: right as drafted.
notes: The Alaska Defense Command's headquarters at Fort Richardson and Elmendorf Field (opened 1940 to 1941; an airfield in Dec 1941, an air base later). Coal from the Matanuska field on the Alaska Railroad. About 3,500 people in 1940, many more by 1942. Seward's coast guns came 1942.

name: Fairbanks
check: vp 0 makes it a village on the town card though it was Alaska's second town (about 3,500): vp 1 if the map builder wants it a town
notes: Inland: the Alaska Railroad's northern end. Ladd Field, the Army's cold-weather test station (1940), was the handover point of the aircraft flown to the Soviet Union from September 1942; an air base by 1944 with the field at Mile 26. Coal at Healy. Winters to minus 50.

name: Copper River
check: Takes Cordova and, if its line reaches that far east, Yakutat with the Army field built 1940 to 1941; otherwise field_1941 is Cordova's small field (hedged)
notes: Valdez and Cordova are ice-free harbours; the Richardson road ran from Valdez to Fairbanks. The Kennecott copper mines up the Copper River closed in 1938. Heavy snow and rain on the coast.

name: Nome
check: Harbour none: ships lay off Nome and lightered cargo ashore, and only from June to October; feeds_troops 1 on the reading of ruling 179 (supplied by sea at all), with the ice to say when Spot-checked by the historian 17 Nov: right as drafted.
notes: The Seward Peninsula; sea ice from November to June. Nome's field was a staging point for the aircraft flown to the Soviet Union (Marks Field from 1942). Gold country. 82 km of Bering Strait from Siberia at its western cape.

name: Kuskokwim
check: Harbour none: Bethel is reached up the river by shallow boats in summer; feeds_troops 1 for summer barges, or 0 if the map builder keeps the port flag for sea harbours only
notes: The Yukon and Kuskokwim delta: tundra, lakes and bog. Bethel's Army field came in 1942 on the route to the Soviet Union. Ice from October to May.

name: Yukon Flats
notes: The interior along the Yukon: spruce forest, bog and river flats; boats on the river in summer only. Galena's Army field (1942) lies on the Yukon to the west. Among the coldest winters in North America.

name: Arctic Slope
check: feeds_troops 0: one supply ship reached Barrow each summer through the ice; climate entered as subarctic as the list has no polar class
notes: Arctic tundra; little rain or snow all year; sea ice nine to ten months. The Navy's Petroleum Reserve No. 4 (set aside 1923) was explored from 1944 but gave no oil in the war, so oil 0.

name: Bristol Bay
check: Takes the Alaska Peninsula: Cold Bay's great anchorage and its Army field (Fort Randall, built early 1942) lie here if the line runs so; otherwise only the salmon roadsteads of Naknek and Dillingham (harbour none)
notes: Salmon canneries; the Naknek (King Salmon) field came 1942. Cold Bay was the base of the 1945 handover of ships to the Soviet Navy.

name: Kodiak
garrison_1941: Fort Greely (Army) and the naval air station (opened June 1941) (hedged)
history: Never attacked; the Navy's Alaskan headquarters and the North Pacific force's base for the Aleutian campaign, 1942 to 1943
check: Works 1: Fort Greely's and Fort Abercrombie's guns were going in during 1941 and 1942 (hedged: 0 if not ready in December). Ground mountain where the map builder has hills: the island is mountain and fjord Floor (ruling 181) is the clerk's: the planner's file has no value for it. Floor checked by the historian 17 Nov: half, as the clerk proposed.
notes: Women's Bay: the naval operating base and air station, runways and seaplanes (an airfield). Fleet base 1: the North Pacific force was based here in 1942. Historian 17 Nov: floor half: a large island with salmon, game and some cattle, unlike the bare Aleutians.

name: Juneau
check: Juneau was the Territory's seat: a territory is not a government, so capital 0 (as Honolulu); vp 1 for it
notes: The northern panhandle and its islands, with Sitka's naval air station on Japonski Island (1939; seaplanes, and a runway by 1941, hedged) and Juneau's airport (1935). Sitka's coast guns came 1942 to 1943. Rain all year, most in autumn; a temperate rain forest.

name: Ketchikan
check: field_1941 1: the Army field on Annette Island was building through 1941 and took Canadian fighters in 1942 (hedged: 0 if not usable in December)
notes: The southern panhandle's islands; about 5,000 people in 1940. One of the wettest towns in North America.

name: Dutch Harbor
garrison_1941: Fort Mears and the naval operating base (hedged: a few thousand)
history: Bombed by Japanese carriers 3 to 4 June 1942, in the Midway operation; never landed on; Fort Glenn on Umnak, built secretly early 1942, sent the fighters that met the raid
check: Fleet base 0: a base for destroyers and submarines, not a fleet anchorage (the fleet's Aleutian anchorage was Kodiak, then Adak). field_max 2 assumes Umnak folds in Floor checked by the historian 17 Nov: quarter, to match the other Aleutians.
notes: Fog thickest June to August, gales October to March, rain all year. Ground mountain where the map builder has hills: Unalaska is all mountain. Historian 17 Nov: floor quarter: treeless mountain and fog like Attu and Kiska; no farming; fish alone would not feed a garrison of thousands.

name: Adak
garrison_peak: tens of thousands of Americans by 1943 (hedged)
history: Occupied unopposed by America 30 Aug 1942 and its field built in about ten days; the base against Kiska and Attu
check: Chief place: no town stood on Adak in 1941; Kuluk Bay is where the base grew Floor (ruling 181) is the clerk's: the planner's file has no value for it. Floor checked by the historian 17 Nov: quarter, as the clerk proposed (empty, treeless).
notes: Kuluk Bay and Sweeper Cove: the main fleet anchorage of the Aleutians from 1943. Fog, gales, rain all year. Historian 17 Nov: islet 0: about 50 km long, larger than Kiska and near Attu's size (Attu is 0).
